explanation: Fires on subword pieces in the middle of multi-token technical names, especially biochemical enzyme/compound names (the 'osph'/' phosph' in phosphatase, cyclophosphamide, transferrin, integrin, chymotrypsin). It also fires on the first piece of a proper name split into tokens (' Ste' in Stevie/Steiker, ' Tom', ' Fort', ' Techn'). Strongest on phosphatase-type enzyme words; ordinary whole words barely activate it.

Fires on subword fragments inside rare or foreign proper names and non-English words (surnames, place names, Turkish/Estonian/Danish/Greek/Hindi/Japanese text), usually a mid-word piece after an uncommon prefix (Ne[[uner]], Zandvo[[ort]], Lo[[zan]]). Common English words and code tokens give only weak activation.

Fires on function words in fixed multiword patterns where the next token is highly predictable: 'as' in 'X as Y' comparisons (beautiful as well, as big as), 'by' in 'Code generated by', 'under' in 'Licensed under', 'to' in 'Reasons to', and boilerplate code tokens (rgb(, Route path, long_description). It also fires on mid-word pieces of technical words (sepsis, isosulfan). Ordinary prose function words give only weak activation.

Fires on odd formatting tokens in OCR'd or scraped documents: long whitespace runs used for alignment in court headers ('United States Court of Appeals' / 'Circuit'), spaces left where text is missing, garbled OCR characters, and single digits inside numbers or years. Normal prose tokens barely activate it.

Fires on a token between a name or noun and the specifier that follows it, especially the space before a model or version number (Atari[[ ]]7800, OnePlus[[ ]]3, Lupin the[[ ]]3rd, during the[[ ]]1938). It also fires on prepositions or conjunctions in ranges and attachments ('between 1987[[ and]]', 'Bishop[[ of]]', 'trapped[[ in]]'). The activation reflects the role of the slot more than any one token type.

No clear unifying pattern. It fires on diverse tokens: the token after 'Category' in wiki footers (Category[[:]]), pieces inside code paths and identifiers, mid-word fragments of scientific terms (ultracold, near-future, bandpass), and common words in prose ('of the', 'during World'). The only loose common thread is technical or reference contexts.

Fires on the preposition or article that starts a locative or categorizing phrase after a noun, mostly 'in' and 'a' ('species of X[[ in]] the family', 'coffee[[ in]] the world', 'build ... list[[ in]] O(|E|)', 'In[[ a]] sense', 'on[[ a]] world scale'). It is strongest on 'in' right after a noun phrase, weaker on other function words.

Fires on function words and method words in scientific abstracts, mainly physics, biophysics and physiology: prepositions and articles in methods phrases ('studied[[ using]]', 'based[[ on]]', 'coupled[[ to]]', 'ground state of[[ the]]'), plus technical modifiers ('projector[[ augmented]] wave', 'localized[[ surface]] plasmon'). It needs academic-abstract register; the same words in casual text activate it weakly.

Fires on digits inside long reference identifiers, mainly the middle digits of U.S. patent numbers ('U.S. Pat. No. 4,20[[5]],780') and the digits or spaces in legal reporter citations ('774 F.2d[[ ]]456') and DOI-style article IDs. It is weaker on tokens in templated math problems and near zero in ordinary text.

Fires most strongly on '.org' in 'developer.mozilla.org' / 'www.mozilla.org' URLs. It fires moderately on the second subword piece of a word split after a short capitalized first piece (Ren[[al]], Ren[[in]], H[[un]], N[[un]], Re[[yn]]olds), across languages. Digits inside years give weak-to-mid activation.

Fires on subword pieces inside mathematical or scientific proper names and terms, especially the second piece of eponymous or Greek-derived words (Tet[[ration]], F[[ib]]onacci, Mand[[el]]brot, z[[eta]], Fan[[coni]], F[[ib]]roblast). Ordinary words give only weak activation.

Fires on verbs that mean changing, replacing or switching something ('change', 'changed', 'switching', 'replace', 'Restore', 'REMOVE', 'relocating', Russian 'заменить'), most strongly when the verb heads a change of name, id or state. Unrelated verbs and other words give weak activation.

Mixed. It fires on '.' in legal reporter citations ('430 So[[.]]2d'), on subword pieces of names and identifiers in code headers and comments (author names, package names, 'NVIDIA Corporation', 'The Trustees'), and on assorted mid-word pieces and nouns in prose (B[[oto]]x, welter[[weight]], 'the chance'). There is no single shared feature.

Fires on a word that marks which member of a contrasted or related pair is meant, most often a possessive or referring word after 'and'/'that' ('her son', 'and his son', 'my wife'), contrastive modifiers ('upper and lower', 'the latter', 'rural'), and group labels ('Group C', 'USH3)'). It also fires on the opening quote of a nickname. The pattern is loose.

Fires on digits (and nearby tokens like ' a', ' of', ' sq', 's') inside large quantities, especially money amounts in millions or billions ('$1[[0]]0 million', '£15[[0]]m', 'hundreds[[ of]] millions', 'half[[ a]] trillion') and areas ('10,000 sq'). It fires moderately on digits in percentages and measurements and weakly on small counts.

Hard to pin down. It fires strongly on ' =' in JavaScript/Swift variable declarations ('var x[[ =]]'), on words inside quoted speech ('We[['ll]]', 'boost[[ our]]', '“'), on 'How[[ long]]' and 'ago', and on mid-word pieces of names and words (kind[[erg]]arteners, Phil[[har]]monic). These look like unrelated jobs.

Fires on the second token of a fixed, highly predictable multi-token unit: 'look[[ like]]', 'President[[ Obama]]', 'George[[ Washington]]', 'West[[ Virginia]]', 'Long[[ Island]]', '/[[usr]]/bin', 'ASP[[.NET]]', 'Institute[[ of]]', '$this[[->]]'. The more predictable the continuation, the stronger the activation.

Fires on a noun for people that follows a number or quantifier ('killed 90[[ people]]', 'employs 95 people', 'home to 9,800 people', '629 million individuals', 'members', 'inhabitants'). It is strongest for 'people' after an explicit count, weaker for other counted nouns (views, pupils, staffers) or verbs after 'N people' ('died').

Fires on a subword piece inside a compound code identifier in camelCase or snake_case (validate[[CS]]RF, enclave_link[[_l]]ibraries, extract[[Vol]]Chapter, FT_BEGIN[[_HEADER]]), usually the piece that starts a new word part after the first part. Plain prose is near zero.

Fires on words that mark contrast with a previous instance or alternative, most strongly 'time' in 'this time' ('again ..., this time in six games'). It also fires moderately on comparatives and contrast markers ('different', 'albeit', 'but', 'much worse', 'simpler', 'another/other approach', 'just').

No crisp pattern. It fires on a token that completes a predictable phrase in casual or explanatory prose ('a copy[[ of]]', 'be[[ there]]', 'the right[[ thing]]', 'what he said he[[ would]] do', 'well[[ behaved]]', 'sorted[[ out]]'). The tokens vary widely, and the activation reflects predictability in context more than any token identity.
